title: Pillar-first stacking: grow tall nanowire bitlines, then deposit tiers
idea: Worse: drill ever-deeper holes through a finished tier stack until etch aspect ratio caps tier count. Flip: grow the vertical bitline/channel pillars FIRST by templated selective-area epitaxy (bottom-up AR >100 is routine for nanowires), then build the tiers around them with conformal deposition and one blanket CMP per tier, so stack height comes from growth and deposition and no deep etch ever happens.
why: Removes the high-AR etch that blocks manufacturable 3D DRAM (facts 2, 4); tier count no longer capped near 75:1, plausibly 150+ tiers with zero per-tier lithography.

title: Self-rolling Swiss-roll array: one patterned film becomes twenty tiers
idea: Worse: pay a full lithography and alignment cycle for every tier. Flip: pattern one long strained-bilayer (e.g., SiN on Si/SiGe or oxide-semiconductor) thin-film array once, then undercut a release layer so built-in strain rolls it into a tight multi-turn tube whose turns become tiers, with wordlines exiting at the tube ends and bitlines contacted along the outer seam.
why: Tier count is set by roll turns, not litho steps: ~20x footprint density from a single planar mask set; attacks EUV dependence and capital intensity (fact 4).

title: Second array on the wafer backside sharing one periphery
idea: Worse: use only one face of the wafer and grind 700 um of silicon to dust. Flip: after building the front array and bonding to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, build a second low-thermal-budget array on the exposed backside, and tie both arrays to the same sense amps through nano-TSVs so every periphery block serves two arrays.
why: ~2x bits per wafer start and half the periphery area per bit (fact 7: periphery ~49% of die); halves quartz-crucible wafer demand per bit.

title: Periphery sandwich: mature-node CMOS bonded to arrays on both faces
idea: Worse: give every array a private periphery built in the expensive DRAM process. Flip: fabricate a 28 nm-class CMOS periphery wafer with hybrid-bond pads on both faces (via backside nTSVs), bond one cell-only array wafer above and one below, and time-share each sense amp between the upper and lower bitline through an isolation switch.
why: Periphery moves to cheap depreciated nodes and is amortized over two arrays: periphery area per bit -50% and the array wafer becomes cell-only (fact 7, fact 4 capital).

title: Threshold-coded tier select replaces the staircase
idea: Worse: carve a giant staircase so every tier gets its own contact, with area and trim steps growing linearly with tier count. Flip: dope each tier's built-in select transistor to one of several thresholds during in-situ deposition and drive a few shared vertical select gates with a voltage code that turns on exactly one tier, i.e., a binary decoder embedded in the stack.
why: Tier contacts drop from N to ~2*log2(N) lines; saves ~5-10% die area and dozens of trim/etch steps at 64+ tiers (facts 2, 7).

title: Spare tiers with post-stack tier-remapping fuses
idea: Worse: stack tiers or dies blindly so one bad layer scraps the whole stack (yield^N). Flip: build every stack with 1-2 spare tiers and a tier-map fuse ROM in the base die, test after stacking, and logically swap failed tiers out exactly as spare rows are swapped today.
why: HBM stack yield loss is 20-30% (fact 6): 0.97^12 ~69% becomes >95% with two spares at ~15% bit overhead; the same scheme makes 100+ tier monolithic stacks yieldable.

title: Smart-cut tier films with donor-wafer reuse
idea: Worse: consume a full CZ wafer, grown in a Spruce Pine quartz crucible, for every bonded layer and then grind it away. Flip: hydrogen-implant and split a 100-200 nm single-crystal Si film from a donor for each tier, bond it onto the stack, pattern after bonding so alignment is litho-limited, and re-polish and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
why: Single-crystal access transistors in every tier keep the leakage tail low (fact 3) while wafers and crucibles consumed per tier fall ~10-20x (resource chokepoints).

title: Memory on the cold side: thermal-break 3D DRAM beneath logic
idea: Worse: stack DRAM directly on a 700 W accelerator so it bakes at 95 C and refreshes 4x more often. Flip: hybrid-bond the DRAM tiers to the logic through a low-thermal-conductivity bonding interlayer that only signal vias cross, and cool the DRAM from its own backside cold plate while logic heat exits the opposite face.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C; holding DRAM at ~55 C instead of 95 C cuts refresh ~10x (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) while keeping on-logic data-movement savings (fact 5).

title: Micro-row 3D activation: per-tier wordline stubs open 64 bits
idea: Worse: open an 8 KB row for every 64 B request. Flip: in a vertical-wordline 3D array, split each vertical wordline into per-tier stubs behind a local select device at the tier edge, so one activation energizes only one tier of one subarray stripe (64-512 bits).
why: Overfetch falls from 128x to ~1-8x and random-read energy from 5.9 pJ per useful bit to <1 pJ (fact 8); fewer activations also shrink row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Sealed air-gap tiers to slash bitline capacitance
idea: Worse: pack dielectric between cells so bitline parasitics dwarf the cell capacitor. Flip: build tiers with sacrificial carbon or SiGe spacers between lateral cells and bitlines, then remove them through the slit and pinch-seal, leaving k~1 gaps around every bitline.
why: Signal scales with Cs/(Cs+Cbl): cutting Cbl ~40-50% lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF, shortening lateral capacitors and tiers (facts 1, 2) and reducing hammer coupling (fact 9).

title: Floating-plate differential capacitor shared by two stacked cells
idea: Worse: give each cell its own plate electrode, plate contacts and a single-ended half-signal. Flip: place one capacitor dielectric directly between a storage node in tier k and a storage node in tier k+1 so the two access transistors write complementary charge across it, storing one bit differentially with no plate line at all.
why: Doubles sense signal per fF so Cs can roughly halve (fact 1) and removes plate-line wiring and contacts from the 3D stack (fact 2).

title: Unsawn wafer-scale memory slab bonded to a logic wafer
idea: Worse: dice, package and TSV-stack small dies, losing kerf, pads and 20-30% stack yield. Flip: hybrid-bond an entire array wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer, keep it whole, and route around failed tiles with a programmable on-wafer mesh, so no dicing, packaging or HBM TSVs are needed.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, fact 6) and package cost, recovers ~10% area from kerf and pads, and gives <0.5 pJ/bit links versus 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Ge-fraction-coded superlattice: chemistry, not overlay, cuts every cell part
idea: Worse: align each tier's transistor, gate and capacitor regions with separate masks whose overlay drifts tier by tier. Flip: grow all tiers in one epitaxy run with sublayers of different Ge fraction, then from a single vertical slit run composition-selective lateral etches whose recess depth scales with Ge content, so capacitor cavity, gate recess and spacer of every tier are cut in a few etches, self-aligned by chemistry.
why: Per-tier masks and overlay error go to zero (facts 2, 4), so added tiers cost only epitaxy time.

title: Hexagonal vertical bitlines with three cells radiating per tier
idea: Worse: use square grids where each vertical bitline serves cells in only two directions, wasting footprint between capacitors. Flip: place vertical bitlines on a hexagonal lattice with lateral cells radiating at 120 degrees and wordline planes cut into three interleaved phases, so each bitline serves three cells per tier.
why: ~1.4-1.5x cells per footprint per tier in lateral 3D DRAM, i.e., ~30% fewer tiers to hit the 26-tier break-even (fact 2).

title: Helically twisted vertical bitline pairs cancel coupling noise
idea: Worse: run neighboring vertical bitlines in parallel through 100 tiers so their mutual coupling swamps a 5 fF cell signal. Flip: swap the positions of each bitline pair every N tiers through staggered intra-stack crossover vias, so aggressor coupling cancels like a twisted-pair cable.
why: Permits ~20-30% tighter vertical bitline pitch or a smaller Cs at the same sense margin (facts 1, 2).

title: Corrugated capacitor walls from multilayer selective recess
idea: Worse: etch smooth cylinder walls so electrode area grows only with height. Flip: etch capacitor holes through an alternating oxide/nitride (or Si/SiGe) mold and selectively recess every other layer before electrode deposition, giving fin-like corrugated walls that multiply area 2-3x at the same aspect ratio.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall without AR 115 or k 70 (fact 1): ~5 fF at AR ~30-40, which also eases mold collapse.

title: Talbot interference lithography for perfectly periodic array layers
idea: Worse: run a $200M single-source EUV scanner to print what is just a periodic grating. Flip: print the array's hole and line layers with achromatic Talbot or multi-beam immersion interference exposure, whose 'mask' is a cheap grating, and keep DUV only for aperiodic cut and periphery layers.
why: Removes most of the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4); interference tools cost ~5-10x less and have no single-supplier chokepoint.

title: In-situ-doped junctionless channels for buried lateral tiers
idea: Worse: try to implant source/drain into tiers buried 3 um deep where no ion can reach. Flip: dope every channel tier uniformly during epitaxy or deposition and build junctionless gate-all-around access devices that turn off by full depletion, eliminating every per-tier implant and activation anneal.
why: Removes the lateral-transistor doping blocker in 3D DRAM (fact 2) and the dopant-diffusion variability that feeds the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Per-tier back-gate plane biased negative during retention
idea: Worse: let one worst-case leaky cell among billions set the refresh period. Flip: embed a thin conductive back-gate plane under each channel tier as part of the deposited stack and pump it negative during retention to suppress tail leakage, releasing it during access for full drive.
why: Pushing the <=13 fA tail toward ~1 fA could stretch refresh ~10x, cutting the 46 fJ/bit refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax (fact 3).

title: Grounded shield tiers between wordline tiers stop row hammer
idea: Worse: place aggressor wordlines nanometers from victim storage nodes with nothing in between. Flip: insert a thin grounded conductive shield plane between adjacent wordline tiers (one extra deposition per tier pair) that terminates the aggressor field and blocks trap-assisted charge migration between tiers.
why: Raises the hammer threshold from ~1k toward >50k activations (fact 9), allowing cheaper mitigation and a tighter tier pitch.

title: Backside capacitor on a 4F2 vertical-channel cell
idea: Worse: cram capacitor, bitline and wordline onto the same face so they fight over one 4F2 footprint. Flip: build vertical-channel transistors with buried bitlines and the periphery on the front, flip-bond to a carrier, thin from the back, and form the capacitors on the exposed channel bottoms so each capacitor gets the full footprint with no bitline contacts threading between them.
why: Enables true 4F2 (1.5x over 6F2, fact 4) without bitline-capacitor contact conflicts, and decouples the capacitor thermal budget from the transistor.

title: Open tier-stack standard on a shared U.S. pilot line
idea: Worse: keep every company's 3D DRAM base stack secret so each one separately relearns 100-tier deposition, slit etch and staircase. Flip: a U.S. consortium standardizes the base stack (superlattice, slits, staircase, bond interface) as a foundry PDK on a shared pilot line, and members differentiate only on the cell module inserted into it.
why: Splits the $15B+, 3-5 year learning curve (fact 4) across members and builds U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.

title: Monolithic stack whose vertical bitlines replace HBM's TSV die stack
idea: Worse: build 12 separate DRAM dies, each losing area to TSV keep-out zones and microbumps, and stack them. Flip: fabricate one monolithic many-tier array whose vertical global bitlines run through the tiers as native interconnect, bonded once to a logic base die, so the 12-high TSV stack becomes one die and one bond.
why: Removes the ~3x area-per-bit HBM TSV tax and the 20-30% stack-yield loss (fact 6): one bond instead of twelve.

title: Vertical charge-coupled strings: bits march through 128 gate tiers
idea: Worse: give every bit its own access transistor, capacitor and contact. Flip: store bits as charge packets in a vertical CCD channel threaded through a 128-tier stack of 3-phase clocked gate plates, shifting them to one sense/regenerate node at the base, which also refreshes each packet as it recirculates.
why: A bit costs ~3 gate tiers in one hole with no capacitor or per-bit transistor: ~42 bits per 60 nm-pitch hole ~74 nm2/bit versus 864 nm2 for 6F2 at F=12 nm (~11x) with a 3D-NAND-like flow at similar wafer cost; refresh is built in, and 32-stage segments keep latency in the 10-100 ns range.

title: One hole, a hundred capacitors: tier-segmented storage rings
idea: Worse: etch a separate deep hole for every capacitor. Flip: in a lateral-transistor 3D stack, etch one vertical hole per cell column, recess each tier's channel end into a ring-shaped storage node, line the hole with one high-k film and fill it with a single common plate core, so every tier's capacitor is a segment of the same hole.
why: Capacitor etch, dielectric and plate are paid once for N tiers: 100 tiers at ~60F2 footprint per tier-cell gives ~86 nm2/bit (~10x) at deposition-dominated cost similar to today's wafer; the ~1 fF rings require short segmented bitlines (high risk).

title: Convert idle 3D-NAND lines to vertical floating-body DRAM strings
idea: Worse: insist new DRAM capacity needs new $15B DRAM fabs. Flip: toll existing 200+-layer 3D NAND lines (same oxide/nitride stack, channel-hole etch, staircase) to build vertical-channel capacitorless floating-body cells by swapping the charge-trap film for a thin gate oxide and adding a hole-reservoir body contact, then sell DRAM-class strings under take-or-pay tolling contracts.
why: At NAND-class wafer cost, 200 tiers at 1 bit/cell gives ~5-7 Gb/mm2 versus ~0.5 Gb/mm2 for 2D DRAM (>10x) and reuses tools already paid for (fact 4: 3-5 years, $15B); floating-body retention and refresh load are the main risk.

title: Pitch-for-tiers trade: 200-tier DRAM on depreciated DUV fabs
idea: Worse: chase F~12 nm with 5-7 EUV layers on new, fully depreciating tools. Flip: relax the lateral pitch to F~20 nm, which DUV immersion SAQP prints in already-depreciated logic or NAND fabs, and buy density back with ~200 tiers whose added cost is only deposition and a shared etch.
why: A ~40F2 lateral cell at F=20 nm is 16,000 nm2 per tier, so 200 tiers give ~80 nm2/bit (~11x versus 6F2 at 12 nm); with depreciation (~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) mostly gone and no EUV, wafer cost holds flat despite the extra deposition.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 300-tier holes without plasma
idea: Worse: push million-dollar cryogenic plasma etchers past 75:1 one wafer at a time. Flip: pattern a thin Au/Ag catalyst mesh and let metal-assisted chemical etching (HF/H2O2) sink it straight down through a Si/SiGe superlattice in a wet batch bath, producing holes and slits at AR >200 for ~300 tiers.
why: Etch aspect ratio stops capping tier count (facts 2, 4) and a batch wet step costs a fraction of plasma etch, so a 300-tier stack lands near today's wafer cost; at ~60F2 per tier-cell that is ~30 nm2/bit, comfortably >10x.

title: Spatial-ALD carousel deposits ten tiers per wafer pass
idea: Worse: deposit 200 tiers sequentially in chamber-based ALD/CVD so deposition time becomes the new cost wall. Flip: run wafers through rotary spatial-ALD carousels with gas-separated precursor zones that lay down alternating channel/dielectric/sacrificial films at ~10x the throughput per tool, with in-line ellipsometry closing the loop on each tier's thickness.
why: Keeps per-tier deposition at ~0.1-0.2% of wafer cost, so the ~150-200 tiers needed for 10x density add <30% to cost and less capex than chamber tools (fact 4).

title: Atomically thin channel tiers: 250 tiers in the same etch depth
idea: Worse: make each tier 50-70 nm thick so 100 tiers already need a 6 um etch. Flip: shrink tier pitch to ~20 nm by using 1-3 nm channels (ALD In2O3-class oxide or CVD MoS2), 5 nm gate dielectric and thin metal gates, so ~250 tiers fit into the 5-6 um depth that 3D NAND already etches.
why: ~3x more tiers per unit etch depth: 250 tiers at ~60F2 per tier-cell is ~35 nm2/bit (>10x even with 50% array efficiency) at an unchanged etch budget (facts 2, 4).

title: Multi-tier porous-oxide isolation: one bath makes 150 SOI tiers
idea: Worse: get single-crystal channels in every tier by bonding 150 wafers or by fragile SiGe replacement. Flip: grow a p+/p- doping superlattice of single-crystal Si, then electrochemically anodize from the slits so only the p+ layers turn porous, and thermally oxidize the porous layers into insulator, leaving 150 single-crystal Si-on-insulator tiers from one wet step.
why: Crystalline low-leakage channels in all tiers (fact 3) for one anodize+oxidize step instead of per-tier bonding, keeping a 150-tier, 10x-density stack within today's wafer cost.

title: Volumetric holographic exposure patterns thirty tiers at once
idea: Worse: expose, develop and etch each tier separately. Flip: spin a thick (3-5 um) photo-patternable hybrid dielectric, write a 3D holographic interference intensity pattern that cross-links the cavity layout of ~30 tiers in one exposure, develop it into a 3D scaffold, then fill the cavities with ALD channel, high-k and metal.
why: One exposure replaces dozens of patterning steps: three exposures for ~90 tiers give ~10x density at roughly today's lithography budget, with no EUV (fact 4).

title: Band-offset quantum-well bits stacked along a superlattice pillar
idea: Worse: store each bit on a bulky capacitor needing femtofarads. Flip: etch vertical pillars through a Si/Ge-rich superlattice, wrap each Ge-rich well with a tier gate, and store holes in its valence-band well (up to ~0.5 eV offset) as the bit, sensed as a threshold shift of the shared vertical Si channel, which is capacitorless and has no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.
why: Every tier of every pillar is a bit: 128 tiers at 50 nm pillar pitch is ~17 nm2/bit (~50x), so 10x survives even at 20% array efficiency with NAND-like process cost; retention from thermal emission over the band offset is the speculative part.

title: Long lateral capacitors storing two bits per cell
idea: Worse: hold to 1 bit/cell because 5 fF barely yields one clean sense level. Flip: exploit the fact that a 3D lateral capacitor's length is set by a cheap timed recess, make ~20 fF capacitors whose 4x signal supports 4-level (2-bit) storage, and read them with a successive-approximation charge-sharing sense amp under the array.
why: 2 bits/cell halves the tiers needed for 10x: ~60 tiers x 2 bits reaches ~10x density with half the deposition and etch depth (facts 1, 2), keeping wafer cost flat.

title: One wordline plate gates two channel tiers: shared double-gate stack
idea: Worse: give every channel tier its own wordline tier and isolation, so each bit costs ~3 films of stack height. Flip: build repeating channel/gate/channel/isolation units where each metal wordline plate gates the channel above and the channel below, with upper and lower channels routed to alternate vertical bitlines so the two cells stay independently addressable.
why: Stack height per bit falls ~35%, so ~1.5x more tiers fit the same etch: a 100-tier-depth etch holds ~150 effective tiers, enough for ~10x at unchanged etch and similar deposition cost.

title: Advance market commitment paying only for 10x-density, cost-parity DRAM
idea: Worse: subsidize fab floor space that just replicates 6F2 DRAM. Flip: a U.S. government plus hyperscaler buyers' club pre-commits to buy a fixed volume (e.g., 10 EB) at today's $/wafer-equivalent only from parts with >=10x bits/mm2 versus 1-gamma DRAM, paying milestone premiums for tier-yield results and nothing for raw capacity.
why: A pull incentive aimed exactly at the 10x-density, same-cost target that de-risks the 3-5 year, $15B bet (fact 4) for whichever 3D architecture wins, and anchors the output in U.S. fabs.

title: Epitaxial thyristor cross-point decks: no capacitor, no access transistor
idea: Worse: build a capacitor plus a transistor for every bit. Flip: grow p-n-p-n layers and self-align-etch them into cross-point pillars between orthogonal word and bit lines so each crossing is a gated bistable thyristor cell, and stack 12 decks where every line layer serves the deck above and below.
why: 4F2 per deck at F=16 nm (DUV SAQP) across 12 decks is ~85 nm2/bit (~10x), patterned with ~13 DUV line masks, roughly the cost of the 4-5 EUV layers it replaces (fact 4).

title: Wedge-polished ramp exposes all tiers to one contact mask
idea: Worse: build the staircase with one resist-trim/etch cycle per tier pair so contact cost grows linearly with tiers. Flip: taper a narrow band at the array edge to a ~5 degree ramp with angled CMP or ion-beam polishing, exposing every tier as a ~0.5 um stripe on the slope, then land all tier contacts with a single DUV mask.
why: Staircase cost becomes O(1) instead of O(N), so scaling from 30 to 300 tiers (the 10x lever) adds deposition but no staircase steps or trim cycles (facts 2, 4, 7).

title: In-stack gain tiers segment vertical bitlines every 32 tiers
idea: Worse: hang 300 tiers of cells on one vertical bitline so its capacitance buries the signal and forces a sense amp per short column. Flip: insert a 'gain tier' every 32 tiers containing a local charge-to-current amplifier and a segment switch on each vertical bitline, so a 1-2 fF cell sees only its 32-tier segment and one base sense amp serves the whole column.
why: Lets Cs drop ~3x and tiers grow 10x without growing periphery (fact 7: ~49% of die), so die cost holds flat at 10x bits.

title: Hot-wall batch epitaxy grows a hundred superlattice wafers per run
idea: Worse: grow 200-period Si/SiGe stacks one wafer at a time for hours in single-wafer RPCVD. Flip: grow the superlattice in a hot-wall UHV-CVD/LPCVD batch furnace holding ~100 wafers, using fast gas-pulse switching for abrupt interfaces and in-situ X-ray reflectometry on a witness wafer.
why: Epitaxy cost per wafer for a 200-tier stack falls ~30-50x, keeping the 10x-density stack inside today's wafer cost envelope (facts 2, 4).

title: Contactless whole-wafer self-test keeps test cost flat at 10x bits
idea: Worse: probe-test 10x more bits per die serially so test time and probe-card capex scale 10x. Flip: power every die on the wafer inductively or through on-die photovoltaic pads, run built-in self-test of all tiers in parallel, read pass/fail maps through an optical or RF backchannel, and program tier and row spares in the same pass.
why: Test (~5-10% of DRAM cost) stays flat while bits per die grow 10x, so the density gain is not eaten by test capex (capital intensity).

title: RAID across tiers: one parity tier per sixteen
idea: Worse: let one defective tier among 200 kill or degrade the die. Flip: write each 16-tier group with an XOR parity tier computed in the base die and reconstruct a failed tier's bits on read, so random tier defects become correctable instead of becoming yield loss.
why: At 200 tiers, tier-defect yield^N would wreck cost per good bit; ~6% parity overhead holds die yield near 2D levels, so 10x density survives at the same cost (facts 2, 6).

title: Replacement capacitor: 200 placeholders swapped for high-k through the slit
idea: Worse: finish each tier's capacitor before building the next, so early tiers suffer every later anneal and every tier pays its own dielectric step. Flip: leave a sacrificial SiN placeholder at each tier's capacitor site, complete the whole stack, then through the slits exhume all placeholders and deposit electrode, high-k and plate into all 200 tiers in one ALD sequence, like NAND gate replacement.
why: Capacitor cost becomes ~O(1) in tier count and thermal budget stops accumulating (facts 1, 2), letting ~200 tiers reach 10x at near-2D wafer cost.

title: Metal-induced lateral crystallization from bitline holes seeds all tiers
idea: Worse: accept leaky poly channels in deposited tiers or pay for 200 epitaxial or bonded layers. Flip: deposit cheap a-Si tiers, drop a Ni or Al nucleant into the vertical bitline holes, and anneal at ~500 C so crystallization fronts grow laterally from each hole along every tier at once, giving near-single-grain channels exactly where the access transistors sit, then strip the nucleant.
why: Near-crystalline leakage tails (fact 3) at deposited-film cost from one anneal, so 100-200 cheap tiers deliver 10x density at roughly 2D wafer cost; metal contamination control is the risk.

title: Folded U-cell stacks transistor over capacitor inside one tier
idea: Worse: lay the access transistor and capacitor end to end so lateral 3D cells run ~2x longer than the bitline pitch needs. Flip: build each tier as two sublayers where the channel runs out from the bitline in the upper sublayer, turns down through a self-aligned via at the far end, and the capacitor runs back underneath toward the bitline.
why: Halves lateral cell length for ~1.5x taller tiers, ~1.4x net density per etch depth, so 10x needs ~30% fewer tier-depth microns at the same cost (facts 1, 2).

title: Orthogonal-per-tier cells cut by two alternately opened slit families
idea: Worse: point every tier's cells the same way so adjacent bitline columns must sit a full cell length apart. Flip: alternate two sacrificial materials by tier and open X-slits and Y-slits at different times, each selectively recessing one material, so even tiers' cells run along X and odd tiers' along Y and neighboring columns interleave into each tier's vacant quadrants.
why: Packs ~1.5x more cells per footprint per tier with no extra masks beyond the second slit, so 10x is reached at ~80 tiers instead of ~120 at the same cost (fact 2).
